architectural_implications.after: Agent runs linting, compiler, unit tests, and its own criteria-based review before handing off; humans review architecture and functionality only.
architectural_implications.before: Agent generates code; the first correctness signal comes from a human reviewer at the end of the pipeline.
architectural_implications.consequence: Human review capacity is preserved by design, and the gatekeeper burnout pattern is mitigated; verification tooling becomes the critical path for adoption velocity.
architectural_implications.observation: Verification moves from a terminal human review stage into the agent's own execution loop via deterministic checks and self-review.

architectural_implications.after: Tests are authored first as the goal contract; the agent is driven from red to green against them.
architectural_implications.before: Tests exist to catch regressions after code is written by a human.
architectural_implications.consequence: Investment in test infrastructure and coverage becomes a prerequisite for safe agent delegation, and spec plus acceptance criteria collapse into one artifact.
architectural_implications.observation: The test suite becomes the primary interface for specifying agent work rather than only a regression net.

architectural_implications.after: Artifacts start with a short human-written summary/intent followed by AI-generated detail, with AI content marked.
architectural_implications.before: PR descriptions, docs, and messages are assumed to be human-authored and read uniformly.
architectural_implications.consequence: Readers calibrate reading time and skepticism per section; provenance labeling becomes a required property of communication pipelines.
architectural_implications.observation: Generated artifacts need an explicit human-intent layer at their head so readers can separate intent from elaboration.

architectural_implications.after: Engineers tag the agent in Slack, meeting them where they are working.
architectural_implications.before: Agent invocation lives in a dedicated tool or IDE session engineers must switch into.
architectural_implications.consequence: Lower invocation friction increases usage frequency, which raises the importance of upstream verification and cost controls.
architectural_implications.observation: The agent is surfaced in the channel where engineers already operate rather than requiring a separate surface.

core_insights.generalization: Any system where an agent produces artifacts faster than humans can audit them needs an explicit ordered verification ladder with cost-weighted routing from cheap automated checks to expensive human judgment.
core_insights.insight: Verification should be structured as a tiered pyramid with distinct owners: deterministic analysis (linting, compiler, unit tests) first, then agent self-review against explicit criteria, then human review reserved for architecture, functionality, and high-level decisions. The speaker frames verification investment as the single highest-leverage organizational action — i.e., the bottleneck to agent productivity is validation capacity, not generation capacity.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes the agent harness as primarily a validation pipeline: work should be routed upward through cheap deterministic gates before it ever consumes human attention. Teams that instead scale generation without scaling verification create a review bottleneck downstream.

evidence_quotes.text: Playwright MCP and automated test suites allow agents to explore and verify code independently.
Empower agents with ways to validate their own work and shift validation left in the development lifecycle.

core_insights.generalization: Agent harness design should prioritize equipping agents with the same executable oracles a human engineer would use (test runners, linters, browser automation, type checkers) so correctness signal is available at generation time rather than review time.
core_insights.insight: Giving the agent executable feedback surfaces (Playwright MCP, automated test suites) so it can explore and validate its own work is presented as a concrete mechanism for closing the loop inside the agent runtime, rather than deferring all feedback to human reviewers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The agent's reliability depends on having tools that return ground-truth signals about its own output. Handing the agent a browser-driving MCP server and a runnable test suite converts verification from a human post-process into an in-loop, machine-checkable step.

core_insights.generalization: For long-horizon agent tasks, investing in an explicit, durable spec artifact can pay back multiplicatively because it amortizes across generation and review, and constrains the search space the agent explores.
core_insights.insight: Plan-before-prompt is a concrete workflow inversion: engineers write detailed implementation plans before invoking agents, which both prevents agent drift and puts the engineer back in the driver's seat. The reported result is that a week spent on a detailed plan yielded 5x speedups in implementation and review cycles.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It relocates the human's high-value contribution to specification time and away from post-hoc correction. The claim that review cycles also sped up matters: the plan serves as shared context that makes generated code legible to reviewers, not just as a prompt artifact.

core_insights.why_it_matters: It supplies the agent with a binary, machine-checkable objective that both constrains generation and doubles as the acceptance gate — combining spec and verification in one artifact rather than two.

core_insights.generalization: When generation cost drops, human review and context-holding roles become the scarce resource and degrade first; agent rollouts should be designed around protecting those roles rather than around maximizing generation throughput.
core_insights.insight: A named failure mode of naive adoption: engineers caught in prompt-and-react cycles lose job satisfaction and agency, while senior engineers holding the context absorb disproportionate burnout as gatekeepers blocking bad AI PRs. The resistance to agent adoption is therefore a predictable consequence of bad workflow design, not tool skepticism.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It predicts where adoption breaks organizationally and points to two distinct fixes: restore specification/authoring control to individual engineers, and reduce the volume of low-quality artifacts reaching senior reviewers via upstream verification.

deep_dives.why: If verification is the highest-leverage investment, teams need cost-weighted routing data to decide where to add gates rather than guessing. Without per-tier catch and escape rates, 'invest in verification' is unfalsifiable advice and the pyramid stays a diagram instead of a control structure.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Giving the agent executable feedback surfaces (Playwright MCP, automated test suites)
deep_dives.why: It distinguishes two architectures for the same outcome: verification as in-loop machine-checkable signal versus verification as a human post-process. The measurable delta (review iterations, revert rate) determines whether harness investment should go into tooling the agent can execute or into downstream reviewer capacity.

deep_dives.why: A single week-long anecdote conflates two mechanisms with different engineering consequences: if the gain is prompt-side drift reduction, invest in spec authoring tools; if the gain is reviewer legibility, invest in artifact conventions and PR structure. Both imply 5x is not a property of planning per se.

key_claims.evidence: Spending a week on a detailed plan yielded 5x speedups in implementation and review cycles.
key_claims.verification_question: Is the 5x figure reproducible across teams and task sizes, and what part of the gain comes from the plan versus from reviewer context sharing?

key_claims.claim: Prompt-and-react cycles reduce engineer job satisfaction and agency, driving resistance to agent adoption.

project_ideas.measurement: Human review iterations per merged change; agent PR rejection rate; revert rate; time-to-merge.

project_ideas.based_on: Spending a week on a detailed plan yielded 5x speedups in implementation and review cycles.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Splitting the plan-first gain into a generation-side component and a reviewer-side component will show that plan artifacts improve review speed even when the agent receives no plan, i.e. a material share of the reported speedup comes from reviewer legibility rather than drift reduction.
project_ideas.measurement: Implementation time, review cycle count, rework rate, and reviewer comprehension time, attributed per condition.
project_ideas.name: Plan-Artifact Ablation
project_ideas.poc: Four-condition comparison across matched tasks: no plan, plan given to agent only, plan given to reviewer only, plan given to both. Measure implementation time, review cycles, and rework rate per condition.

source.title: How to Get Your Org to Adopt Coding Agents (Without Shipping Garbage) — Eyal Blum, Figma

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Eyal Blum
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Internal organizational adoption of coding agents at Figma while maintaining high code quality and developer satisfaction.
  • Purpose: To provide engineering leadership with actionable frameworks, strategies, and lessons learned on how to successfully scale coding agent adoption across an organization while maintaining high quality standards and developer morale. Eyal Blum, a software engineer at Figma, shares the internal journey of adopting coding agents into engineering workflows without compromising code quality. He outlines the three-act journey of AI adoption—the honeymoon phase, the crash, and mastering the real skill of AI usage. The talk addresses friction points like reduced developer agency, burnout among top engineers, and communication inflation, offering actionable lessons on verification, planning over prompting, treating feedback from skeptics as a roadmap, and attention-aware communication.

Topic Map

The Three-Act AI Adoption Journey

  • Explanation: Organizations go through three phases when adopting coding agents: the honeymoon phase where simple tasks work 10x faster; the crash where complex workflows fail, bugs slip through, and trust breaks down; and the real skill phase where proper planning and verification amplify human judgment.
  • Key claims:
    • Simple tasks work 10x faster in the honeymoon phase.
    • Complex workflows fail and erode trust during the crash phase.
    • Real skill involves proper planning, verification, and correct guardrails.
  • Examples:
    • Trying to apply simple prompting practices to bigger problems resulting in bad code and bugs.
  • Terminology:
    • Honeymoon phase
    • The crash
    • Real skill
  • Why it matters: Understanding this trajectory helps organizations anticipate burnout and resistance, guiding teams past the initial crash into mature AI usage.

Organizational Friction Points

  • Explanation: AI adoption creates distinct friction points: uneven adoption across teams, reduced developer agency, burden on top engineers acting as gatekeepers, and ineffective communication caused by AI-generated noise.
  • Key claims:
    • Adoption is uneven across different engineering teams.
    • Engineers experience reduced job satisfaction when stuck in prompt-and-react cycles.
    • Top engineers absorb disproportionate burnout acting as gatekeepers for bad AI code.
    • Design docs, Slack messages, and emails increase in volume without a corresponding increase in clarity.
  • Examples:
    • Top engineers holding all context and getting burnt out by blocking bad AI PRs.
  • Terminology:
    • Developer agency
    • Gatekeepers
    • Uneven adoption
  • Why it matters: Recognizing these friction points is essential for engineering leaders to design interventions that protect team morale and code quality.

Lessons Learned at Figma: Verification and Planning

  • Explanation: To succeed, organizations must invest in verification, shift-left validation, test-driven development (TDD), and rigorous planning before prompting agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Investing in verification is the highest-value thing an organization can do.
    • Left-shifting validation moves verification earlier in the workflow and down the testing pyramid.
    • TDD with agents leads to significantly better results because goals are defined before code is written.
  • Examples:
    • Using test-driven development where the agent is told to write code from red to green.
  • Terminology:
    • Shift-left validation
    • Test-driven development (TDD)
    • Verification pyramid
    • Deterministic analysis
  • Why it matters: Shifting from unstructured prompting to structured planning and verification unlocks massive productivity gains without shipping garbage.

Culture and Communication in the Age of AI

  • Explanation: Attention is a scarce resource in the age of AI. Organizations must build new communication cultures that clearly distinguish AI-generated content from human-authored content and meet engineers where they are already working.
  • Key claims:
    • Human attention is a scarce resource when AI generates abundant artifacts.
    • Marking AI versus human-generated content helps calibrate reading time and skepticism.
    • Meeting engineers where they are working (e.g., tagging agents in Slack) reduces friction.
  • Examples:
    • Adding human-written summaries at the top of PR descriptions followed by AI-generated details.
  • Terminology:
    • Attention-aware communication
    • Source clarity
    • Comms culture
  • Why it matters: Establishing clear communication protocols prevents communication fatigue and restores trust across engineering teams.

Key Points

Invest in Verification

  • Explanation: Empower agents with ways to validate their own work and shift validation left in the development lifecycle.
  • Evidence: Playwright MCP and automated test suites allow agents to explore and verify code independently.
  • Practical implication: Reduces human review overhead and catches bugs before code reaches production.

Plan Before You Prompt

  • Explanation: Putting engineers back in the driver's seat by writing detailed implementation plans before invoking agents prevents agent drift.
  • Evidence: Spending a week on a detailed plan yielded 5x speedups in implementation and review cycles.
  • Practical implication: Transforms AI usage from chaotic prompting to structured software engineering.

Treat Skeptics' Feedback as a Roadmap

  • Explanation: Skeptical engineers highlight real tool failures and lack of validation; their feedback is the blueprint for improving AI safety.
  • Evidence: Skeptics get upset when AI code lacks validation, pointing directly to gaps in guardrails.
  • Practical implication: Brings resistant engineers along the journey and hardens internal AI workflows.

Attention-Aware Communication

  • Explanation: Clearly delineate human intent from AI generation in PRs, Slack, and docs to respect scarce human attention.
  • Evidence: PR descriptions starting with human-written intent followed by AI details reduce misunderstandings and friction.
  • Practical implication: Improves signal-to-noise ratio in internal communication channels.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Three-Act AI Adoption Journey

  • How it works: Describes the psychological and operational stages organizations experience when adopting AI tools.
  • Components:
    • Act 1: The Honeymoon (simple tasks 10x faster)
    • Act 2: The Crash (complex work fails, bugs slip, trust breaks)
    • Act 3: The Real Skill (proper planning, verification, and human judgment)
  • When to use: When diagnosing team sentiment and planning organizational AI rollout strategies.

Verification Pyramid

  • How it works: Structures code verification from automated deterministic checks up to human review.
  • Components:
    • Deterministic Analysis (linting, compiler, unit tests)
    • Agent Review (agent validation against criteria)
    • Human Review (architecture, functionality, high-level decisions)
  • When to use: When establishing CI/CD pipelines and guardrails for coding agents.

Plan-Over-Prompt Framework

  • How it works: Shifts effort from interactive trial-and-error prompting to upfront architectural planning.
  • Components:
    • Start with the 'Why' (executive summary)
    • Break it down into small, independently verifiable parts
    • Ensure each part has a validation gate
  • When to use: Before delegating complex coding tasks to autonomous agents.

Examples & Case Studies

An engineer ran an AI analysis tool over PR comments without clearly marking what was human-written versus AI-generated.

  • Illustrates: The friction caused by ineffective communication and lack of source clarity in AI-heavy environments.
  • Lesson: Always explicitly mark AI-generated communication and lead with human intent to maintain trust and respect attention.

An engineer spent a week writing a detailed migration plan, aligned with three teams, and then handed it to an agent for overnight implementation.

  • Illustrates: The power of upfront planning combined with autonomous agent execution.
  • Lesson: Detailed planning followed by agent implementation achieves massive speedups without sacrificing architectural coherence.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Implement test-driven development (TDD) workflows when prompting coding agents.
    • Add human-written introductions to AI-generated PR descriptions and documents.
    • Tag coding agents directly inside Slack workflows where engineers already operate.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift validation left by giving agents tools to execute tests and verify work.
    • Engage skeptical engineers early; their feedback is your roadmap to robust adoption.
    • Build a verification pyramid combining deterministic analysis, agent review, and targeted human review.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can we better measure developer agency and satisfaction alongside productivity?
    • What parts of our codebase lack sufficient deterministic tests for agent self-validation?
    • How do we scale attention-aware communication across the entire enterprise?

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Eyal Blum
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Internal organizational adoption of coding agents at Figma while maintaining high code quality and developer satisfaction.
- **Purpose**: To provide engineering leadership with actionable frameworks, strategies, and lessons learned on how to successfully scale coding agent adoption across an organization while maintaining high quality standards and developer morale.
Eyal Blum, a software engineer at Figma, shares the internal journey of adopting coding agents into engineering workflows without compromising code quality. He outlines the three-act journey of AI adoption—the honeymoon phase, the crash, and mastering the real skill of AI usage. The talk addresses friction points like reduced developer agency, burnout among top engineers, and communication inflation, offering actionable lessons on verification, planning over prompting, treating feedback from skeptics as a roadmap, and attention-aware communication.
## Topic Map
### The Three-Act AI Adoption Journey
- **Explanation**: Organizations go through three phases when adopting coding agents: the honeymoon phase where simple tasks work 10x faster; the crash where complex workflows fail, bugs slip through, and trust breaks down; and the real skill phase where proper planning and verification amplify human judgment.
- **Key claims**:
  - Simple tasks work 10x faster in the honeymoon phase.
  - Complex workflows fail and erode trust during the crash phase.
  - Real skill involves proper planning, verification, and correct guardrails.
- **Examples**:
  - Trying to apply simple prompting practices to bigger problems resulting in bad code and bugs.
- **Terminology**:
  - Honeymoon phase
  - The crash
  - Real skill
- **Why it matters**: Understanding this trajectory helps organizations anticipate burnout and resistance, guiding teams past the initial crash into mature AI usage.
### Organizational Friction Points
- **Explanation**: AI adoption creates distinct friction points: uneven adoption across teams, reduced developer agency, burden on top engineers acting as gatekeepers, and ineffective communication caused by AI-generated noise.
- **Key claims**:
  - Adoption is uneven across different engineering teams.
  - Engineers experience reduced job satisfaction when stuck in prompt-and-react cycles.
  - Top engineers absorb disproportionate burnout acting as gatekeepers for bad AI code.
  - Design docs, Slack messages, and emails increase in volume without a corresponding increase in clarity.
- **Examples**:
  - Top engineers holding all context and getting burnt out by blocking bad AI PRs.
- **Terminology**:
  - Developer agency
  - Gatekeepers
  - Uneven adoption
- **Why it matters**: Recognizing these friction points is essential for engineering leaders to design interventions that protect team morale and code quality.
### Lessons Learned at Figma: Verification and Planning
- **Explanation**: To succeed, organizations must invest in verification, shift-left validation, test-driven development (TDD), and rigorous planning before prompting agents.
- **Key claims**:
  - Investing in verification is the highest-value thing an organization can do.
  - Left-shifting validation moves verification earlier in the workflow and down the testing pyramid.
  - TDD with agents leads to significantly better results because goals are defined before code is written.
- **Examples**:
  - Using test-driven development where the agent is told to write code from red to green.
- **Terminology**:
  - Shift-left validation
  - Test-driven development (TDD)
  - Verification pyramid
  - Deterministic analysis
- **Why it matters**: Shifting from unstructured prompting to structured planning and verification unlocks massive productivity gains without shipping garbage.
### Culture and Communication in the Age of AI
- **Explanation**: Attention is a scarce resource in the age of AI. Organizations must build new communication cultures that clearly distinguish AI-generated content from human-authored content and meet engineers where they are already working.
- **Key claims**:
  - Human attention is a scarce resource when AI generates abundant artifacts.
  - Marking AI versus human-generated content helps calibrate reading time and skepticism.
  - Meeting engineers where they are working (e.g., tagging agents in Slack) reduces friction.
- **Examples**:
  - Adding human-written summaries at the top of PR descriptions followed by AI-generated details.
- **Terminology**:
  - Attention-aware communication
  - Source clarity
  - Comms culture
- **Why it matters**: Establishing clear communication protocols prevents communication fatigue and restores trust across engineering teams.
## Key Points
### Invest in Verification
- **Explanation**: Empower agents with ways to validate their own work and shift validation left in the development lifecycle.
- **Evidence**: Playwright MCP and automated test suites allow agents to explore and verify code independently.
- **Practical implication**: Reduces human review overhead and catches bugs before code reaches production.
### Plan Before You Prompt
- **Explanation**: Putting engineers back in the driver's seat by writing detailed implementation plans before invoking agents prevents agent drift.
- **Evidence**: Spending a week on a detailed plan yielded 5x speedups in implementation and review cycles.
- **Practical implication**: Transforms AI usage from chaotic prompting to structured software engineering.
### Treat Skeptics' Feedback as a Roadmap
- **Explanation**: Skeptical engineers highlight real tool failures and lack of validation; their feedback is the blueprint for improving AI safety.
- **Evidence**: Skeptics get upset when AI code lacks validation, pointing directly to gaps in guardrails.
- **Practical implication**: Brings resistant engineers along the journey and hardens internal AI workflows.
### Attention-Aware Communication
- **Explanation**: Clearly delineate human intent from AI generation in PRs, Slack, and docs to respect scarce human attention.
- **Evidence**: PR descriptions starting with human-written intent followed by AI details reduce misunderstandings and friction.
- **Practical implication**: Improves signal-to-noise ratio in internal communication channels.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Three-Act AI Adoption Journey
- **How it works**: Describes the psychological and operational stages organizations experience when adopting AI tools.
- **Components**:
  - Act 1: The Honeymoon (simple tasks 10x faster)
  - Act 2: The Crash (complex work fails, bugs slip, trust breaks)
  - Act 3: The Real Skill (proper planning, verification, and human judgment)
- **When to use**: When diagnosing team sentiment and planning organizational AI rollout strategies.
### Verification Pyramid
- **How it works**: Structures code verification from automated deterministic checks up to human review.
- **Components**:
  - Deterministic Analysis (linting, compiler, unit tests)
  - Agent Review (agent validation against criteria)
  - Human Review (architecture, functionality, high-level decisions)
- **When to use**: When establishing CI/CD pipelines and guardrails for coding agents.
### Plan-Over-Prompt Framework
- **How it works**: Shifts effort from interactive trial-and-error prompting to upfront architectural planning.
- **Components**:
  - Start with the 'Why' (executive summary)
  - Break it down into small, independently verifiable parts
  - Ensure each part has a validation gate
- **When to use**: Before delegating complex coding tasks to autonomous agents.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An engineer ran an AI analysis tool over PR comments without clearly marking what was human-written versus AI-generated.
- **Illustrates**: The friction caused by ineffective communication and lack of source clarity in AI-heavy environments.
- **Lesson**: Always explicitly mark AI-generated communication and lead with human intent to maintain trust and respect attention.
### An engineer spent a week writing a detailed migration plan, aligned with three teams, and then handed it to an agent for overnight implementation.
- **Illustrates**: The power of upfront planning combined with autonomous agent execution.
- **Lesson**: Detailed planning followed by agent implementation achieves massive speedups without sacrificing architectural coherence.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Implement test-driven development (TDD) workflows when prompting coding agents.
  - Add human-written introductions to AI-generated PR descriptions and documents.
  - Tag coding agents directly inside Slack workflows where engineers already operate.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift validation left by giving agents tools to execute tests and verify work.
  - Engage skeptical engineers early; their feedback is your roadmap to robust adoption.
  - Build a verification pyramid combining deterministic analysis, agent review, and targeted human review.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can we better measure developer agency and satisfaction alongside productivity?
